lessons.title: Colorado brokerage relationships and disclosures
lessons.body:
## Why Colorado is different

Most national textbooks teach agency as the default: a licensee who works with a buyer or seller is that person's agent unless something says otherwise. Colorado flips this. Colorado's brokerage relationships law (C.R.S. 12-10-401 and following) gives you three ways to work with a party, bans a fourth, and sets a default you must memorize.

| Relationship | Who the broker works for | Advocate? | Written agreement needed? |
|---|---|---|---|
| [[Seller's agent]] / landlord's agent | Only the seller or landlord | Yes | Yes, before brokerage activity |
| [[Buyer's agent]] / tenant's agent | Only the buyer or tenant | Yes | Yes, before brokerage activity |
| [[Transaction-broker]] | One or both parties, as a facilitator | No | Not to create the relationship (it's presumed), but a written disclosure is required, and any seller or landlord listing must be in writing |
| [[Dual agency]] | Both sides as agents | Not allowed | Prohibited by statute |

## Single agency

A [[single agent]] is a broker engaged by, and representing, only one party. The statute names four single agents: seller's agent, buyer's agent, landlord's agent and tenant's agent. Colorado calls a single agent a [[limited agent]]: the agent's duties are the ones listed in the statute plus any extra duties the parties add in a written contract. Single agency exists only when there is a written agreement with the party being represented, signed before the broker begins brokerage activities for that party.

A single agent may cooperate with other brokers, but may not engage or create [[subagents]]. Old-style "subagency," where every MLS member worked for the seller, is not available in Colorado.

## Transaction-brokerage: the presumed relationship

A transaction-broker helps one or more parties through a transaction (communication, advice, negotiation, contract terms and closing) without being an agent or advocate for anyone.

The key rule: **a Colorado broker is presumed to be a transaction-broker unless a single agency relationship is established by a written agreement.** If a Commission listing or buyer contract leaves the relationship boxes blank, the broker works with the client as a transaction-broker, consistent with the statute.

> **Exam tip:** "No written agency agreement" in a Colorado question almost always points to transaction-broker, not "implied agency" or "no relationship."

## Dual agency is prohibited

Colorado statute says a broker shall not act as a dual agent. Written consent from both sides does not fix it. National-exam answers like "dual agency is legal with informed written consent of both parties" are wrong for the Colorado portion.

## Customers vs. clients

A [[customer]] is a party to a transaction who has not engaged or employed the broker, so there is no brokerage relationship with that person. A party who has engaged the broker, as a single agent or as a transaction-broker, is commonly called the broker's client.

A broker who works for one side may still help the other side's customer with [[ministerial tasks]], once the relationship has been properly disclosed. Examples: showing the property, acting as a scrivener (filling in the form), passing along offers and counteroffers, explaining financing options, and giving information about inspectors, lenders and other services. These tasks do not create an agency or transaction-broker relationship with the customer.

## Required disclosures and their timing

### The written disclosure

Colorado requires brokerage relationships to be disclosed in writing. The Commission rule sets the timing: the written disclosure must be made **before the broker elicits or discusses confidential information** from the consumer (for example, motivation or financial qualifications). The Division describes this as the earliest reasonable opportunity.

What does *not* trigger the requirement: preliminary small talk about price range, location and property style, and answering general factual questions about a property advertised for sale or lease.

The statute adds specifics:

- **Transaction-broker:** before engaging in brokerage activities, disclose in writing that the broker is not the party's agent and is acting as a transaction-broker.
- **Single agent:** sign a written agency agreement with the party before engaging in brokerage activities.
- **Seller's agent working with a buyer:** before engaging in brokerage activities with the buyer, give a written disclosure that the broker is the seller's agent and not the buyer's agent, list the tasks the broker will do for the seller in dealing with the buyer, and state that the buyer is not vicariously liable for the agent's acts.
- **Other parties:** a broker who has a relationship with one party must tell the other parties (or their brokers) about it at the earliest reasonable opportunity.

### Which document makes the disclosure

The disclosure is made on Commission-approved forms:

- When the broker has a signed engagement contract (for example, an exclusive right-to-sell listing or an exclusive right-to-buy contract), that contract states that different brokerage relationships are available and identifies the relationship chosen.
- When the broker works with someone without an engagement contract, the broker uses the matching [[brokerage disclosure]] form: Brokerage Disclosure to Buyer, to Tenant, to Seller (for sale by owner) or to Landlord. These forms include the definitions of the relationships, a box for the relationship (for example, the party is a customer, or the broker is a transaction-broker), and an acknowledgment of receipt.

These disclosures include a signature block so the party can acknowledge receipt. The acknowledgment is **not a contract**. If the party refuses to sign, the broker notes the refusal (and the date) on a copy and keeps that copy, along with the email that delivered the form if it was sent electronically.

> **Exam tip:** Timing is the most tested point. The written disclosure comes **before confidential information is elicited or discussed**. It does not wait for a signed contract, and it is not triggered only by the consumer's questions.

### Definitions of Working Relationships

The Commission-approved [[Definitions of Working Relationships]] form defines seller's agent, buyer's agent, transaction-broker and customer, and states that it is not a contract. Keep two separate rules straight:

1. **The relationship disclosure is always required.** Every broker must disclose the relationship in writing before eliciting or discussing confidential information (see above). The firm's written disclosures must also state that buyer agency, seller agency and transaction-brokerage are available.
2. **The Definitions form is required in one specific situation.** A firm does not have to offer every relationship, but its written office policy must say which ones it offers. If a party asks about a relationship the firm does **not** offer, the broker must give that party the Commission's written definition of it, which is what this form is for. Otherwise the form is a reference for explaining the options.

The Division states that the definitions section of this form is **not, by itself, a brokerage disclosure**. Handing a consumer only this form doesn't satisfy the written disclosure rule.

> **Exam tip:** Firms may choose not to offer single agency. They must still tell consumers that the other relationships exist, must give the Commission's definition if asked about one they don't offer, and must still make the written relationship disclosure before discussing confidential information.

## Working with both sides: change of status

What if the listing broker's own buyer wants to buy the listing? Under Commission rules, one broker (or one team) may **not** be a single agent for one party while being a single agent or transaction-broker for the other. That is dual agency. With proper written disclosure (usually in the listing contract), the broker or team may instead:

1. act as a transaction-broker for both parties;
2. act as a transaction-broker for one party and treat the other as a customer; or
3. act as a single agent for one party and treat the other as a customer.

If the broker moves from single agent for one party to transaction-broker for both, the broker must give the party whose relationship changes the Commission-approved [[Change of Status]] form. It is due when the broker starts assisting both parties as a transaction-broker, and **no later than when that party signs the contract**. The listing and buyer contracts let the client check a box refusing this option ("seller agency only" or "buyer agency only"). If they do, the other party stays a customer. The change applies only to that transaction: when it ends, the broker's relationship with the client automatically goes back to the one designated in the listing contract.

## Designated brokerage and imputed knowledge

In a firm with more than one licensee, the [[employing broker]] designates in writing which broker or brokers will work with a party. The relationship is **only with the [[designated broker]]**. It does not extend to the employing broker, other brokers in the firm, or the firm itself, and the written agreement must say so. A firm made up of a single licensed person has no designated brokerage; the person and the firm are treated as one.

Results of designated brokerage:

- Two different designated brokers in the same firm may be single agents for opposite sides of the same deal. That is **not** dual agency for the employing broker.
- When a designated broker acts as a single agent, that broker's knowledge is **not** imputed to non-designated brokers ([[imputed knowledge]] does not apply) in the firm.
- In transaction-brokerage, information is not imputed between the broker and a party, or among people within the firm.
- Teams: every team member must be a designated broker for the consumer in the same capacity, and all team members must be named in the listing contract.
- The employing broker may substitute or add designated brokers, and must tell the consumer.
- The Commission treats it as a conflict of interest when an employing broker supervises designated brokers on both sides of a deal and a client's confidential information is shared with the employing broker (or when the employing broker represents one side while supervising the designated broker on the other). Brokers have a continuing duty to disclose known conflicts of interest in writing.

## The employing broker's role

The employing broker must:

- adopt a written office policy (the [[office policy manual]]) describing the relationships the firm offers, how brokers are designated, and how confidential information is protected. Each associate broker gets a copy and signs for it;
- supervise associate brokers (with a higher level of supervision for new brokers) and unlicensed staff;
- maintain the firm's trust accounts and transaction records.

The employing broker may supervise a transaction and also be the designated broker in it. Designated brokerage does not reduce the employing broker's duty to supervise or the firm's [[vicarious liability]]. Clients, however, are not vicariously liable for a broker's acts they did not approve, direct or ratify, and the broker must tell them so.

## How long a relationship lasts

A brokerage relationship begins when the party engages the broker and lasts until the engagement is completed. If it is not completed, it ends at the earliest of the agreed expiration date, termination by the parties, or one year after it began. Commission rules separately require every listing or written brokerage agreement to have a definite termination date. After the relationship ends, a single agent must still account for money and property received, and keep confidential any information the party asked to keep confidential (unless the party consents in writing, the law requires disclosure, or the information becomes public). A transaction-broker's remaining duty is to account for money and property.

lessons.title: Broker duties, disclosures and engagement contracts
lessons.body:
## The duty lists you must know

Colorado spells out broker duties in statute, so the exam can ask about them word for word. Learn the three lists side by side.

### Single agent (seller's agent or buyer's agent)

A single agent must:

1. Perform the terms of the written agreement with the client.
2. Exercise reasonable skill and care.
3. Promote the client's interests with the utmost good faith, loyalty and fidelity, including:
   - seeking a price and terms acceptable to the client (a seller's agent need not seek more offers while the property is under contract; a buyer's agent need not look for other properties while the buyer is under contract);
   - presenting all offers to and from the client in a timely manner, even if the property is already under contract;
   - disclosing [[adverse material facts]] actually known by the broker;
   - counseling the client on material benefits or risks the broker actually knows;
   - advising the client to get expert advice on material matters beyond the broker's expertise;
   - accounting in a timely manner for all money and property received;
   - telling the client it is not vicariously liable for the broker's acts it did not approve, direct or ratify.
4. Comply with the license law and Commission rules.
5. Comply with applicable federal, state and local laws, including fair housing and civil rights laws.

### Transaction-broker

A transaction-broker is not an agent for either party. The duties are to:

1. Perform the terms of any **written or oral** agreement with any party.
2. Exercise reasonable skill and care, including:
   - presenting all offers and counteroffers in a timely manner, even while the property is under contract;
   - advising the parties about the transaction and suggesting expert advice on material matters beyond the broker's expertise;
   - accounting promptly for all money and property received;
   - keeping the parties fully informed;
   - helping the parties comply with the contract terms and close;
   - disclosing to buyers or tenants adverse material facts actually known (title, physical condition, defects, environmental hazards the law requires disclosed);
   - disclosing to sellers or landlords adverse material facts actually known about the buyer's or tenant's financial ability to perform and whether the buyer intends to occupy the property as a principal residence;
   - telling the parties they are not vicariously liable for the broker's acts.
3. Comply with the license law, Commission rules and applicable laws, including fair housing and civil rights laws.

> **Exam tip:** Loyalty, advocacy and "promoting the interests" belong only to single agents. A transaction-broker's skill-and-care list focuses on *process*: present offers, keep parties informed, help them close.

## Confidential information

Each broker type is barred from disclosing certain information without [[informed consent]]:

| Broker | May NOT disclose without informed consent |
|---|---|
| Seller's agent | Seller will accept less than asking price; seller's motivation; seller will accept other financing terms; material information about the seller (unless required by law or withholding it would be fraud or dishonest dealing); facts or suspicions that could psychologically impact the property |
| Buyer's agent | Buyer will pay more than the offered price; buyer's motivation; buyer will accept other financing terms; material information about the buyer (same exceptions); psychological-impact facts |
| Transaction-broker | All of the above, for any party. Here the informed consent must come from **all parties** |

## What a seller's agent owes the buyer

A seller's agent owes the buyer no duties except one: disclose adverse material facts about the property that the broker **actually knows**, such as title problems, physical condition, material defects and environmental hazards the law requires disclosed. The seller's agent has **no duty to independently inspect** the property for the buyer and no duty to verify the accuracy of statements made by the seller or by independent inspectors.

## What a buyer's agent owes the seller

A buyer's agent owes the seller no duties except to disclose adverse material facts actually known, which **includes facts about the buyer's financial ability to perform and whether the buyer intends to occupy the property as a principal residence**. The buyer's agent has no duty to investigate the buyer's finances for the seller, and no duty to verify the buyer's statements.

## Adverse material facts

The Commission treats an adverse material fact as a fact a reasonable person would consider significant and that works against a party's interest, the kind of fact that could change a decision. Examples the Commission gives: structural problems, environmental or health hazards, building or zoning violations, liens and other title problems, and problems with a buyer's ability to qualify.

The trigger is **actual knowledge**. A broker is not disciplined under this duty for facts the broker merely "should have known" through investigation. If a broker isn't sure whether a known physical fact is material, the Commission recommends disclosing it. The broker's own disclosure duty runs alongside the seller's separate duty to disclose on the Commission's contract forms.

## Psychologically impacted property

Under C.R.S. 38-35.5-101, these facts or suspicions are **not material facts** that must be disclosed:

- an occupant had, or was suspected of having, HIV, AIDS or another disease that medical evidence shows is highly unlikely to be transmitted through occupying a dwelling;
- the property was the site of a homicide, another felony, or a suicide.

No lawsuit may be brought against a broker for failing to disclose these. On top of that, an agent for the owner may **not** disclose such facts without the client's informed consent. The Commission encourages brokers to ask their client for consent to disclose. Psychological-impact facts never excuse hiding a physical adverse material fact. If a crime caused physical damage, the damage is still disclosed.

> **Exam tip:** "Must the seller's agent tell the buyer about a murder in the home?" No, and without the seller's informed consent, the agent may not.

## Things that are NOT breaches

- A seller's agent may show buyers other properties and may list competing properties.
- A buyer's agent may show the same property to competing buyers and help them try to buy it.
- A transaction-broker may do all of the above, and may act as agent or transaction-broker for the same or different people in other transactions.
- No broker type may create subagents.

## Compensation rules

Colorado's statute separates *who pays* from *who is represented*:

- Compensation may come from the seller, buyer, landlord, tenant, a third party, or a split between brokerages. **Paying a broker does not, by itself, create an agency relationship.**
- The parties must be told who will pay the broker **before** they sign a brokerage agreement or a contract to buy, sell or lease.
- A buyer's agent needs the buyer's **written** approval before proposing to the seller's agent that the buyer's agent be paid from the seller's compensation.
- A broker may be paid by more than one party only if those parties consent in writing before entering the contract.

## Listing and buyer agency contracts

- Brokers must use Commission-approved forms when an appropriate one exists. Key engagement forms include the [[exclusive right-to-sell listing contract]], exclusive right-to-buy contract, exclusive right-to-lease and exclusive tenant contracts.
- A seller or landlord listing must be **in writing before any brokerage services are performed**, whatever the relationship. If the seller or landlord refuses to sign a listing contract, the broker may not perform brokerage services for them. Single agency for a buyer also requires a written agreement before brokerage activities.
- Every listing or written brokerage agreement must have a **definite termination date**.
- Each form has check boxes for single agency or transaction-brokerage. **If neither box is checked, the broker is a transaction-broker.**
- The current forms print in capitals that brokerage compensation is **not set by law and is fully negotiable**.
- In the exclusive right-to-sell form, paying part of the fee to a buyer's brokerage is something the listing firm *may* agree to do. It is optional.
- In the exclusive right-to-buy form, the buyer can choose to have the seller or seller's brokerage pay the buyer's brokerage, with the buyer paying the rest. The buyer owes an unpaid amount only if the broker disclosed it in writing before the buyer signed the purchase contract. The buyer's brokerage may not take extra compensation from the seller side without the buyer's written consent.
- [[Holdover]] (protection-period) clauses can cover only people or properties the broker negotiated with during the listing and whose names or addresses were given to the client **in writing** during the listing term.
- A broker must give copies of documents to the parties when they are prepared.
- **Residential engagement contracts (C.R.S. 12-10-403.5):** a written contract that makes a residential seller, buyer, landlord or tenant a broker's client may not run with the land or bind future owners, may not let the broker assign the right to provide services without notice to and agreement of the owner, and may not create a lien, encumbrance or other recordable interest in the property (any such interest is void). Offering a consumer a contract with one of these terms is a deceptive trade practice. Property management agreements are exempt.
- A licensee buying, selling or leasing for their own account must disclose in writing that they are licensed, and brokers must disclose known conflicts of interest in writing.

lessons.title: Trust accounts and earnest money
lessons.body:
## Money belonging to others

Any money a broker receives that belongs to someone else (earnest money, rents, tenant security deposits, money collected in advance for services) is **money belonging to others**. It never belongs to the broker or the firm, and Colorado treats mishandling it as one of the most serious license violations. The statute lists as grounds for discipline: failing to account for or remit others' money within a reasonable time, [[commingling]] it with the broker's own money, converting it, and failing to keep it in a proper escrow or trust account.

## Account requirements

A broker's [[trust account]] (the rules say "trust or escrow account") must:

- be **separate** from the broker's and firm's own money;
- be held at a [[recognized depository]] **in Colorado**: a bank, savings and loan or credit union whose deposits are insured by the FDIC or NCUA (the statute requires a depository "in this state" insured by a federal agency);
- be identified as a fiduciary account in the bank's deposit agreement by using the word **"trust" or "escrow"** plus its purpose, for example "sales escrow," "rental escrow" or "security deposit escrow." The firm keeps a copy of each signed deposit agreement for Commission inspection;
- be in the **firm's name**: an LLC, corporation or partnership uses the entity's name; a sole proprietorship uses the employing broker's name. The employing broker must have authority to withdraw funds. Others may be authorized to sign, but that doesn't shift the employing broker's responsibility;
- keep funds **available immediately without penalty**. No CDs or other fixed-term or early-withdrawal-penalty investments unless the parties agree otherwise in writing.

A properly set-up fiduciary account protects the funds from the broker's creditors: garnishments, lawsuits, bankruptcy and bank setoffs against the broker should not reach them. A firm may have any number of trust accounts, including **zero** if it never holds others' money (for example, when a title company always holds earnest money).

### Property management: two kinds of accounts

A firm that does property management must keep **rents** and **security deposits** in separate trust accounts: at least one account for rental receipts and at least one for security deposits.

### Interest-bearing accounts

Trust funds may be in an interest-bearing account, as long as they stay available immediately without penalty. The Commission's position is that, absent a specific written agreement to the contrary, interest earned on a trust account does **not** belong to the brokerage firm. The purchase contract should say which party gets interest on earnest money, and the management agreement and lease should say who gets interest on rents and security deposits. Keeping it without agreement would be undisclosed compensation.

## Deposit deadlines

| Type of money | Deposit deadline |
|---|---|
| Property management funds (rents, security deposits) | Within **5 business days** after receipt or after the lease is mutually executed, whichever is **later** |
| All other money belonging to others, including [[earnest money]] the firm holds | Within **3 business days** after receipt or after the contract is mutually executed, whichever is **later** |

**Example:** A purchase contract is mutually executed Monday. The buyer hands the listing firm the earnest money check Tuesday. The later event is Tuesday, so the firm must deposit by Friday (3 business days, assuming no holidays).

An associate broker who receives money must turn it over to the employing broker as soon as practicably possible.

> **Exam tip:** 3 business days for sales/earnest money; 5 business days for property management money. Both run from receipt or mutual execution, *whichever is later*.

## Earnest money

The purchase contract names the **[[earnest money holder]]**: usually the listing brokerage or a title (closing) company.

- A broker who receives earnest money must deliver it to the earnest money holder named in the contract and get a **dated, signed receipt**.
- If the brokerage firm is the holder, it deposits the money in its trust account within the 3-business-day rule.
- The firm may later transfer the earnest money to the closing company or attorney handling the closing, again getting a dated, signed receipt.
- If a promissory note is accepted as earnest money, the seller must be told when the note is due. If it isn't paid when due, the broker must promptly tell the seller and give the seller the original note.

### Releasing earnest money and disputes

The Commission's position: when the parties agree on how earnest money should be paid out, the holder should disburse it as they direct without unnecessary delay. The Commission does not itself require signatures from both parties on a release. If one party authorizes in writing that the money go to the other, that's enough. The firm may not demand a release that holds it harmless or waives its liability; the Commission's rules prohibit such exculpatory terms.

When the parties disagree, the brokerage follows the contract. The Commission won't discipline a firm for holding disputed funds as the contract directs. The current residential contract lets the holder keep holding the money, file an [[interpleader]] action asking a court to decide, or (after written notice and no lawsuit within the contract's waiting period) return it to the buyer. If the title company or attorney holds the earnest money, the brokerage is not responsible for how that holder disposes of it. If the party entitled to the funds can't be found, the money may eventually go to the State Treasurer under the Unclaimed Property Act.

> **Exam tip:** A broker who keeps disputed earnest money "as a commission," or releases it to one side because they think that side is right, is wrong. Follow the contract.

## Commingling and conversion

- **Commingling**: mixing the broker's or firm's own money with money belonging to others.
- **Conversion** / diversion: using one beneficiary's money for another beneficiary, or for the broker or firm.

Limited situations where firm money may be in the account:

- the firm may deposit its own funds to cover **bank charges** on the account (recorded in the records);
- the firm may advance its own money for a client (for example, to pay a repair bill) if it is labeled as an advance and recorded.

Money that becomes payable to the firm (earned commissions or management fees) must be **withdrawn monthly**. Fees are earned only when the contracted services are complete and nobody can still claim the money, unless a written agreement says otherwise.

## Security deposit transfers

When a property's management changes firms, the new firm must disclose the status of the security deposits to the owner and tenant in writing within 30 days, and the prior firm must transfer the deposits within 60 days. A firm may hand a security deposit to the owner only if the lease authorizes it in writing or the tenant gets written notice of who holds it.

## Reconciliation and reports

Each trust account needs a **[[journal]]** (chronological record of all receipts and disbursements) and a **[[ledger]]** for each beneficiary. No ledger may show a negative balance, and the ledger total must equal the journal after each posting. Every month the firm performs a [[three-way reconciliation]]: on the same date, the **journal balance**, the **total of all ledger balances**, and the **reconciled bank balance** must agree. The firm keeps a written monthly reconciliation report.

Property management firms report to owners as their management agreement says. If it's silent, reports are due within 30 days after the end of the month in which money was received or paid out. Each branch office with its own trust account needs its own records, and the employing broker is jointly responsible with the firm for all of it.

lessons.title: Record keeping, retention and Commission audits
lessons.body:
## Why records matter

Every brokerage activity leaves a paper (or digital) trail the Commission can inspect. Record keeping is a stated item on the state exam outline, and the rules are short enough to memorize.

## Two kinds of required records

### 1. Trust account records

For each [[trust account]], the [[employing broker]] keeps, at the firm's place of business:

- the **[[journal]]**: a chronological list of every receipt (date, payer, which person and property it relates to, purpose, amount, running balance) and every disbursement (date, check or electronic transfer record, payee, reference to supporting documents, amount, running balance);
- a **[[ledger]]** for each beneficiary, showing the same details, with no negative balances;
- the **monthly [[three-way reconciliation]]** report (journal = ledger total = reconciled bank balance);
- bank statements and a copy of each signed **deposit agreement** showing the account is a trust or escrow account;
- written **accounting control policies** describing the firm's checks and balances over people who handle money.

Supporting documents (invoices, bids, contracts) back up every disbursement in a property management account. The cash method of accounting is the default unless the firm and the owner agree otherwise in writing.

### 2. Transaction files

Each broker and brokerage keeps a [[transaction file]] for every transaction. The Commission publishes a **Transaction File Checklist** listing what must be in sales and property management files: contracts and listing agreements, brokerage disclosures, amendments, notices, closing statements and so on. A firm may require more. The Division recommends, but does not require, keeping related emails and texts.

After closing, the Commission does **not** require you to keep copies of existing public records, title commitments, loan applications, lender-required disclosures, or affirmations from independent closing entities.

## The four-year rule

Required records must be kept for **four years**. The license law states the four-year period, and the Commission rule sets when it starts:

- from the date the transaction **closed** (was consummated), or
- if it never closed, from the date the **listing contract expired**.

> **Exam tip:** Colorado's retention period is 4 years. Watch for 3- and 5-year distractors, and remember the clock starts at closing or listing expiration, not at the date the file was opened.

A broker stays responsible for keeping their transaction files even after moving to a new brokerage.

## Closing responsibility and copies

The broker who has a brokerage relationship with a party is responsible for that party's closing. The party gets a complete, detailed closing statement signed by the broker, and a copy goes to the brokerage firm right after closing. The broker reviews the closing documents and attends closing or is reasonably available. A substitute broker may attend, sharing responsibility. Brokers must also give parties copies of documents they prepare at the time they prepare them, and signed copies of the listing and sale contracts.

## Electronic records

Any required record may be kept electronically. The conditions:

- the record must remain **retrievable** and able to be **printed legibly** for the whole four years;
- electronic or printed copies must be produced when the **Commission** or any **principal party** to the transaction asks;
- a technical problem with the storage system is **not** an excuse. You must still produce the records.

Trust-account journals, ledgers, reconciliation reports and bank statements may also be kept electronically.

## Commission access, investigations and audits

- The Commission may inspect required records, and trust account records are expressly subject to **Commission audit**.
- A broker or firm notified of a complaint or of selection for an audit must respond **in writing by the Commission's deadline**. The response must address each allegation and question and include the complete transaction file and any requested records.
- **Not responding on time is itself grounds for discipline**, even if the underlying complaint has no merit. The Commission grants reasonable requests for extensions.
- Records reasonably needed for an investigation or audit must be kept and produced on time.

## Who is responsible

The **employing broker** (or an independent broker running a one-person firm) is responsible for:

- maintaining trust accounts and trust records;
- maintaining transaction records;
- writing the firm's office policies, including a written policy for disposing of documents that contain personal identifying information;
- supervising associate brokers and unlicensed staff (bookkeepers, assistants) who touch files or money.

The employing broker is jointly responsible with the firm for following the trust account rules. A firm with a branch office that keeps its own trust account must keep separate records for that branch, still under the employing broker's responsibility.

## Quick review

| Item | Colorado rule |
|---|---|
| Retention period | 4 years |
| Clock starts | Closing date, or listing expiration if no closing |
| Format | Paper or electronic |
| Electronic condition | Retrievable and legibly printable; produce on request |
| Who can demand records | Commission; any principal party |
| Reconciliation | Monthly, three-way |
| Failure to answer Commission | Grounds for discipline on its own |

questions.stem: A Colorado broker begins helping a buyer find a home. They have not signed any written agreement. What relationship does Colorado law presume?
choices: Buyer's agent
Transaction-broker
Seller's subagent
No relationship until an offer is written
questions.explanation: Colorado presumes a broker is a transaction-broker unless a single agency relationship is established by a written agreement. Implied buyer agency and subagency are not Colorado defaults.

questions.stem: Under Colorado law, a broker may act as a dual agent for both buyer and seller:
choices: only with the informed written consent of both parties
only if the employing broker approves in writing
never, because Colorado statute prohibits dual agency
only in commercial transactions
questions.explanation: C.R.S. 12-10-406 says a broker shall not act as a dual agent. Written consent does not make it allowed in Colorado, even though many other states permit consented dual agency.

questions.stem: When must a Colorado broker give a consumer the written brokerage relationship disclosure?
choices: Before eliciting or discussing the consumer's confidential information
Within 3 business days after the first meeting with the consumer
When the consumer signs a contract to buy or sell a property
At the first face-to-face meeting, before showing the consumer any property
questions.explanation: Commission rules require the written disclosure before the broker elicits or discusses confidential information such as motivation or finances. Small talk about price range, location or style does not trigger it.

questions.stem: Broker Maria is the seller's agent on a listing. A buyer she also works with as a buyer's agent wants to purchase that listing. The seller did not check the seller-agency-only box. To work with both, Maria must give the Change of Status disclosure no later than:
choices: the date the listing contract expires or ends
the closing of the transaction
the contract's earnest money deadline
the time the consumer signs the contract
questions.explanation: Under the Commission's rule, a broker who moves from single agent for one party to transaction-broker for both must give the Commission-approved Change of Status form to the consumer whose relationship changes, when the broker begins assisting both parties and no later than when that consumer signs the contract.

questions.stem: A broker is the seller's agent on a listing. An unrepresented buyer wants to make an offer through the same broker. Which arrangement is permitted in Colorado?
choices: Seller's agent for the seller and buyer's agent for the buyer
Seller's agent for the seller and transaction-broker for the buyer
Seller's agent for the seller, treating the buyer as a customer
Dual agent for both, with written consent
questions.explanation: Commission rules let one broker be a single agent for one party and treat the other as a customer, with proper written disclosure. A broker cannot be a single agent for one side and an agent or transaction-broker for the other.

questions.stem: In a multi-broker firm, Broker A is the designated seller's agent and Broker B is the designated buyer's agent on the same transaction. Which statement is correct?
choices: The employing broker becomes a dual agent and the deal must be cancelled
It's allowed; it isn't dual agency, and A's knowledge isn't imputed to B
Both brokers automatically become transaction-brokers for both parties
The firm itself becomes the agent of both parties, so knowledge is shared
questions.explanation: With designated brokerage, the relationship is only with the designated broker, so two designated brokers in one firm may be single agents for opposite sides without dual agency. A designated single agent's knowledge is not imputed to non-designated brokers.

questions.stem: A seller tells her listing agent, "I'd take $20,000 less if I had to." A buyer's agent asks whether the seller would accept less. Without the seller's informed consent, the listing agent:
choices: may not disclose that the seller would accept less
must disclose it because it is an adverse material fact
may disclose it if the buyer is preapproved
must disclose it if asked directly
questions.explanation: A seller's agent may not disclose, without informed consent, that the seller will accept less than the asking price. That is confidential information, not an adverse material fact.

questions.stem: A listing broker actually knows the basement floods every spring. The seller tells the broker not to mention it. What should the broker do?
choices: Keep quiet, because the seller's instructions control the agent
Disclose it only if a buyer specifically asks about water or flooding
Disclose it to buyers; it's an adverse material fact she actually knows
Withdraw from the listing without saying anything to buyers or the seller
questions.explanation: A seller's agent owes buyers the duty to disclose adverse material facts actually known about the property. A client's instruction cannot override that statutory duty.

questions.stem: A seller's agent learns that a homicide occurred in the listed house several years ago. The seller has not given permission to discuss it. Under Colorado law:
choices: the agent must disclose it on the Seller's Property Disclosure form
it isn't a material fact, and she can't disclose it without the seller's consent
the agent must disclose it to buyers who are relocating from out of state
the agent must report it to the Commission and note it in the MLS listing remarks
questions.explanation: C.R.S. 38-35.5-101 says the site of a homicide, other felony or suicide is not a material fact requiring disclosure. A seller's agent may not disclose such psychological-impact facts without the client's informed consent.

questions.stem: A buyer's agent knows that her buyer's loan was just denied and the buyer has no other way to pay. What duty does the buyer's agent have toward the seller?
choices: None, because a buyer's agent owes the seller no duties of any kind
To keep it confidential as material information about the buyer client
To tell the seller only if the seller's agent asks about it in writing
To disclose it, as it bears on the buyer's ability to perform
questions.explanation: A buyer's agent must disclose to the seller adverse material facts actually known, including facts about the buyer's financial ability to perform. That duty is an exception to the general confidentiality about the buyer.

questions.stem: After closing, a buyer discovers a cracked sewer line. The seller's agent did not know about it and never inspected the line. Did the agent breach a statutory duty?
choices: No; there's no duty to inspect, only to disclose facts actually known
Yes; listing brokers must inspect all major systems before marketing
Yes; brokers are liable for anything they reasonably should have known
No, but only because the buyer chose to get a home inspection
questions.explanation: Colorado brokers must disclose adverse material facts they actually know. The statute expressly says there is no duty to independently inspect the property or verify statements by the seller or inspectors.

questions.stem: Which duty does a Colorado transaction-broker owe to the parties?
choices: Promote the seller's interests with utmost loyalty
Negotiate the lowest price for the buyer
Keep the parties fully informed regarding the transaction
Seek additional offers while the property is under contract
questions.explanation: Keeping the parties fully informed is a listed transaction-broker duty. Loyalty and advocacy belong to single agents, and a transaction-broker is not an agent for either party.

questions.stem: A transaction-broker is working with both buyer and seller. To disclose that the buyer would pay more than the offered price, the broker needs:
choices: the buyer's verbal permission only
the informed consent of all parties
the employing broker's approval
no consent, because a transaction-broker owes no confidentiality
questions.explanation: A transaction-broker may not disclose that a buyer will pay more, or that a seller will accept less, without the informed consent of all parties.

questions.stem: A broker represents a seller as a single agent and treats the buyer as a customer. Which help may the broker give the buyer without creating a brokerage relationship?
choices: Advising the buyer on how much to offer for the property
Negotiating repair requests on the buyer's behalf with the seller
Telling the buyer the lowest price the seller has said she would accept
Showing the property and filling in the contract form as a scrivener
questions.explanation: Ministerial tasks such as showing property, acting as a scrivener, conveying offers and explaining financing options do not create a relationship with a customer. Advising or negotiating for the buyer would be advocacy, and revealing the seller's lowest price breaches confidentiality.

questions.stem: A seller's agency relationship has ended because the listing expired. What duty does the broker still owe the former seller?
choices: Keep confidential what the seller asked to keep confidential, with exceptions
Continue marketing the property for 30 days under the listing's holdover clause
Present any offers that come in after the listing expires
None; all of the broker's duties end when the listing expires
questions.explanation: After a single agency relationship ends, the broker must still account for money and property and keep confidential information the client asked to be kept confidential, unless the client consents in writing, the law requires disclosure, or it becomes public.

questions.stem: A buyer's agent would like to be paid out of the compensation the seller pays the listing brokerage. Before proposing this to the seller's agent, the buyer's agent must:
choices: get the seller's written consent
get the Commission's approval
obtain the buyer's written approval
convert to transaction-broker status
questions.explanation: Under C.R.S. 12-10-410, a buyer's agent must obtain the buyer's written approval before proposing to the seller's agent that the buyer's agent be paid from the seller's compensation. Payment by the seller side does not by itself create agency with the seller.

questions.stem: A broker uses the Commission-approved Exclusive Right to Sell Listing Contract but leaves both relationship boxes (Seller Agency and Transaction-Brokerage) unchecked. What relationship results?
choices: Seller agency
None; the contract is void
Dual agency
Transaction-brokerage
questions.explanation: By statute, a Colorado broker is presumed to be a transaction-broker unless single agency is established by a written agreement, and the listing form itself says the broker works with the seller as a transaction-broker if neither box is checked. An unchecked box doesn't void the contract or create agency.

questions.stem: A listing contract includes a holdover clause. After the listing expires, the seller sells to a buyer the broker had shown the house to. For the holdover clause to apply under Commission rules, the broker must have:
choices: given the seller that buyer's name in writing during the listing term
recorded the listing contract with the county clerk and recorder
kept the sign in the yard throughout the holdover period
notified the Commission in writing of each prospect shown during the term
questions.explanation: Holdover clauses may cover only persons the broker negotiated with during the listing whose names were given to the client in writing during the listing term.

questions.stem: A purchase contract is mutually executed on Monday. The listing brokerage, named earnest money holder, receives the buyer's check on Tuesday. Assuming no holidays, the brokerage must deposit it by the end of:
choices: Wednesday
Thursday
Friday
the following Tuesday
questions.explanation: Earnest money held by a firm must be deposited within 3 business days after receipt or mutual execution, whichever is later. The later event is Tuesday, so the deadline is Friday.

questions.stem: A property management firm receives a tenant's security deposit. Within what time must it be deposited?
choices: Within 5 business days after receipt or lease execution, whichever is later
Within 3 business days after receipt, as with earnest money
Within 24 hours after the firm receives the deposit
Within 3 business days after receipt or lease execution, whichever is earlier
questions.explanation: Property management funds have a 5-business-day deadline, measured from receipt or mutual execution of the lease, whichever is later. The 3-business-day rule applies to other money, such as earnest money.

questions.stem: A brokerage that manages rental properties for owners must keep:
choices: all rents and deposits in one combined trust account
rents and deposits in one trust account, with a separate ledger for each owner
at least one trust account for rents and a separate one for security deposits
security deposits in certificates of deposit for each tenant
questions.explanation: Commission rules require a property management firm to keep rental receipts and security deposits in separate trust or escrow accounts. Trust funds must also stay available without penalty, which rules out CDs absent written agreement.

questions.stem: Which account setup meets Colorado trust account requirements for an LLC brokerage?
choices: A personal savings account in the employing broker's own name at an out-of-state credit union
A money market fund labeled 'broker reserve' and held in the firm's name
An account at an uninsured investment firm, opened in the name of a client
An account in the LLC's name at an FDIC-insured Colorado bank, labeled trust or escrow
questions.explanation: The account must be at a federally insured recognized depository in Colorado, identified as trust or escrow, and held in the firm's name (the entity's name for an LLC).

questions.stem: A broker leaves several months of earned commissions sitting in the firm's trust account "as a cushion." This is:
choices: permitted, as long as the cushion amount stays under $1,000
commingling; money payable to the firm must be withdrawn monthly
conversion, but only once the firm actually spends the money
required, so the firm can cover future bank charges on the account
questions.explanation: Mixing the firm's own money with money belonging to others is commingling, and money payable to the firm must be withdrawn monthly. Firm money may be in the account only in narrow cases, such as funds to cover the account's bank charges or a recorded advance made for a beneficiary; a 'cushion' isn't one of them.

questions.stem: In a monthly three-way reconciliation, which three figures must agree as of the same date?
choices: Journal balance, total of all beneficiary ledgers, and reconciled bank balance
Bank statement balance, the firm's operating account balance, and the MLS sales report
Gross commissions, net commissions, and broker splits
Earnest money receipts, closing statements, and title commitments
questions.explanation: A three-way reconciliation proves that the journal, the total of the ledgers, and the reconciled bank balance all match. Colorado requires it monthly for each trust account holding money belonging to others.

questions.stem: A sale never closed, and the listing contract expired on March 1, 2026. Under Colorado's record retention rule, the broker must keep the transaction file until at least:
choices: March 1, 2027
March 1, 2029
March 1, 2030
March 1, 2031
questions.explanation: Colorado requires records to be kept for four years, measured from closing or, if there is no closing, from the listing contract's expiration date. March 1, 2026 plus four years is March 1, 2030.

questions.stem: The listing brokerage holds earnest money. The deal falls apart and the buyer and seller each demand the money. What should the brokerage do?
choices: Release it to the seller, since the buyer is the one who walked away
Split it equally between the buyer and seller so neither side can sue the firm
Keep it as the firm's commission until the parties settle
Follow the contract, such as continuing to hold it or interpleading it
questions.explanation: The Commission will not discipline a brokerage that holds disputed earnest money as the contract directs. The Commission-approved contract lets the holder keep holding it, interplead it to a court, or follow the contract's notice procedure. A broker may not decide the dispute or keep the money.

questions.stem: A buyer at an open house starts telling a broker about her finances and why she must move quickly. She has signed nothing with the broker. Which statement about the broker's disclosure duty is correct?
choices: Handing her the Definitions of Working Relationships form by itself satisfies the disclosure rule
The broker must give a written brokerage relationship disclosure before discussing this information
No written disclosure is needed until she signs an exclusive right-to-buy contract
A written disclosure is required only if she asks about a relationship the firm doesn't offer
questions.explanation: Commission rules require the written brokerage relationship disclosure before the broker elicits or discusses confidential information such as finances or motivation. The Definitions of Working Relationships form is required only when a party asks about a relationship the firm doesn't offer, and the Division says its definitions section is not, by itself, a disclosure.

cards.front: Colorado default (presumed) brokerage relationship?
cards.back: Transaction-broker, unless a single agency relationship is created by written agreement.

cards.front: Is dual agency legal in Colorado?
cards.back: No. C.R.S. 12-10-406 bars a broker from acting as a dual agent, even with consent.

cards.front: Four types of single agent in Colorado
cards.back: Seller's agent, buyer's agent, landlord's agent, tenant's agent.

cards.front: What is a 'limited agent'?
cards.back: A single agent whose duties are only those in the statute plus any extra duties agreed in writing.

cards.front: Customer (Colorado)
cards.back: A party who has not engaged the broker, so no brokerage relationship exists with that party.

cards.front: Timing of the written brokerage relationship disclosure
cards.back: Before eliciting or discussing the consumer's confidential information (earliest reasonable opportunity).

cards.front: What does NOT trigger the brokerage disclosure?
cards.back: Small talk about price range, location and property style, and general factual questions about advertised properties.

cards.front: Consumer refuses to sign the relationship disclosure. Broker does what?
cards.back: Notes the refusal and date on a copy and keeps the copy.

cards.front: Is the signed brokerage disclosure a contract?
cards.back: No. The acknowledgment of receipt is not a contract.

cards.front: When must the Definitions of Working Relationships definition be given?
cards.back: Only when a party asks about a relationship the firm doesn't offer (C.R.S. 12-10-408). It does not replace the written relationship disclosure, which is always required before confidential information is discussed.

cards.front: Change of Status form: when used?
cards.back: When a broker moves from single agent for one party to transaction-broker for both.

cards.front: Change of Status form: deadline
cards.back: When the broker begins assisting both as transaction-broker, and no later than when the consumer signs the contract.

cards.front: Same broker, both sides: three permitted options
cards.back: TB for both; TB for one + other as customer; single agent for one + other as customer (with written disclosure).

cards.front: Same broker, both sides: forbidden option
cards.back: Single agent for one party and single agent or transaction-broker for the other.

cards.front: Ministerial tasks for a customer (examples)
cards.back: Showing property, scrivener, conveying offers, explaining financing, info on services. These create no relationship.

cards.front: Designated broker
cards.back: Broker designated in writing by the employing broker to work with a party. Relationship doesn't extend to the employing broker, other brokers or the firm.

cards.front: Two designated brokers in one firm represent buyer and seller as agents. Dual agency?
cards.back: No. Allowed under designated brokerage.

cards.front: Is a designated single agent's knowledge imputed to others in the firm?
cards.back: No. It is not imputed to non-designated brokers.

cards.front: Teams and designated brokerage
cards.back: All team members are designated in the same capacity and must be named in the listing contract.

cards.front: Can a Colorado agent create subagents?
cards.back: No. Single agents and transaction-brokers may cooperate with other brokers but may not create subagents.

cards.front: Single agent duty list (core)
cards.back: Perform written agreement; reasonable skill and care; promote interests with utmost good faith, loyalty and fidelity; follow license law; follow fair housing and other laws.

cards.front: Transaction-broker skill-and-care duties
cards.back: Present offers; advise and suggest experts; account for money; keep parties fully informed; help comply with contract and close; disclose adverse material facts; vicarious-liability notice.

cards.front: Transaction-broker performs which agreements?
cards.back: Any written or oral agreement with any party.

cards.front: Seller's agent may NOT disclose (without consent)
cards.back: Seller will take less; motivation; other financing terms; material info about seller; psychological-impact facts.

cards.front: Buyer's agent may NOT disclose (without consent)
cards.back: Buyer will pay more; motivation; other financing terms; material info about buyer; psychological-impact facts.

cards.front: Transaction-broker confidentiality consent requirement
cards.back: Informed consent of ALL parties.

cards.front: Buyer's agent must disclose to seller
cards.back: Adverse material facts actually known, incl. buyer's financial ability to perform and intent to occupy as principal residence.

cards.front: Duty to independently inspect or verify?
cards.back: None. Brokers disclose adverse material facts they actually know.

cards.front: Psychologically impacted property (C.R.S. 38-35.5-101)
cards.back: HIV/AIDS or other disease highly unlikely to transmit by occupancy; homicide, other felony or suicide. Not material facts, and no lawsuit for nondisclosure.

cards.front: Does paying a broker create agency?
cards.back: No. Payment alone does not create an agency relationship.

cards.front: Buyer's agent paid from seller's compensation: requirement
cards.back: Buyer's written approval before proposing it to the seller's agent.

cards.front: Duration if engagement not completed
cards.back: Ends at earliest of agreed expiration, termination, or one year after engagement.

cards.front: Duties surviving end of single agency
cards.back: Account for money and property; keep requested confidential info confidential (unless exception).

cards.front: Listing contract timing
cards.back: Seller/landlord listing must be in writing before any brokerage services, with a definite termination date.

cards.front: Listing/buyer form with no relationship box checked
cards.back: Broker is a transaction-broker.

cards.front: Compensation statement on Commission listing and buyer forms
cards.back: Compensation charged by brokerage firms is not set by law and is fully negotiable.

cards.front: Earnest money deposit deadline (firm holds it)
cards.back: Within 3 business days after receipt or mutual execution of the contract, whichever is later.

cards.front: Property management funds deposit deadline
cards.back: Within 5 business days after receipt or mutual execution of the lease, whichever is later.

cards.front: Trust account location and insurance
cards.back: Recognized depository in Colorado, insured by FDIC or NCUA.

cards.front: Trust account labeling
cards.back: Deposit agreement uses "trust" or "escrow" plus purpose, e.g. "rental escrow."

cards.front: Whose name is on the trust account?
cards.back: The brokerage entity's name (or the employing broker's name for a sole proprietorship).

cards.front: Property management account separation
cards.back: At least one account for rents and at least one for security deposits.

cards.front: Firm funds allowed in trust account
cards.back: Funds to cover bank charges, and labeled advances for a client. Earned fees must be withdrawn monthly.

cards.front: Interest on trust funds: who gets it?
cards.back: Not the brokerage firm, absent a specific written agreement. The contract, management agreement or lease should say which party gets it.

cards.front: Three-way reconciliation
cards.back: Monthly: journal balance = total ledgers = reconciled bank balance.

cards.front: Record retention period
cards.back: 4 years from closing, or from listing expiration if no closing.

cards.front: Electronic records rule
cards.back: Allowed if retrievable and legibly printable; produce on request of the Commission or a principal party.

cards.front: Failing to respond to a Commission complaint or audit notice
cards.back: Grounds for discipline by itself, even if the complaint lacks merit.

cards.front: Earnest money received by a broker goes to…
cards.back: The earnest money holder named in the contract, with a dated, signed receipt.

cards.front: Does the Definitions of Working Relationships form, by itself, satisfy the disclosure rule?
cards.back: No. Its definitions section alone isn't a disclosure. Use a Commission brokerage disclosure form, or the relationship terms of a signed listing or buyer contract.

cards.front: Brokerage disclosure forms when there's no engagement contract
cards.back: Brokerage Disclosure to Buyer, to Tenant, to Seller (FSBO), or to Landlord: a Commission-approved form that is not a contract.

cards.front: Associate broker receives a check for money belonging to others
cards.back: Place it with the employing broker as soon as practicably possible; the firm then deposits per the 3- or 5-business-day rule.

glossary.definition: A broker engaged by and representing only one party in a transaction: a seller's, buyer's, landlord's or tenant's agent.
A single agent who represents only the seller (listing agent). In leasing, the landlord's agent plays the same role.
A single agent who represents only the buyer. In leasing, the tenant's agent plays the same role.
Colorado's term for a single agent whose duties are only those set by statute plus any additional duties agreed in writing.
A broker who helps one or more parties through a transaction without being an agent or advocate for any of them. Colorado's presumed relationship absent a written agency agreement.
One broker acting as agent for both sides of a transaction. Prohibited in Colorado by statute.
A party to a transaction who has not engaged the broker, so the broker has no brokerage relationship with that party.
Common term for a party who has engaged the broker as a single agent or transaction-broker.
A broker engaged to act for another broker on a principal's behalf. Colorado single agents and transaction-brokers may not create subagents.
A broker the employing broker designates in writing to work with a particular party. The relationship does not extend to the employing broker, other brokers or the firm.
The broker who employs and supervises associate brokers and is responsible for the firm's trust accounts, records and office policies.
Knowledge legally treated as known by someone else. In Colorado, a designated single agent's knowledge is not imputed to non-designated brokers in the firm.

Commission-approved form defining seller's agent, buyer's agent, transaction-broker and customer. Required when a party asks about a relationship the firm doesn't offer. Its definitions alone are not the brokerage disclosure, and it is not a contract.
Commission-approved disclosure given when a broker moves from single agent for one party to transaction-broker for both, no later than when the consumer signs the contract.
Routine help a broker may give a customer, such as showing property, filling in forms, or conveying offers, without creating a brokerage relationship.
A fact a reasonable person would consider significant that works against a party's interest. Brokers must disclose those they actually know.
Property associated with facts like a homicide, other felony or suicide, or an occupant's disease highly unlikely to spread by occupancy. Not material facts under C.R.S. 38-35.5-101.
Permission given after the person understands what will be disclosed or done and its consequences.
Legal responsibility for someone else's acts. Colorado clients are not vicariously liable for broker acts they did not approve, direct or ratify.
The employing broker's written policies describing the relationships offered, how brokers are designated, and how confidential information is protected.
A listing in which the brokerage earns its fee if the property sells during the listing period, no matter who finds the buyer.
A period after a listing or buyer agreement ends during which the broker can still earn compensation from prospects named in writing during the term.
A separate fiduciary account at a recognized depository that holds money belonging to others. Colorado rules call it a trust or escrow account.
Funds a broker holds that are not the broker's own, such as earnest money, rents, security deposits and advance payments.
A bank, savings and loan or credit union insured by the FDIC or NCUA. For Colorado trust accounts it must be in Colorado.
Mixing a broker's or firm's own money with money belonging to others. Prohibited.
Using money belonging to others for the broker's own purposes or for a different beneficiary.
A buyer's good-faith deposit under a purchase contract, held in trust for both parties.
The party named in the contract to hold the earnest money, usually the listing brokerage or a title company.
A court action in which a holder of disputed money deposits it with the court and asks the court to decide who gets it.
A trust account's chronological record of every receipt and disbursement, with a running balance.
A trust account record kept separately for each beneficiary, showing that person's receipts, disbursements and balance.
A monthly check that the journal balance, the total of all ledgers, and the reconciled bank balance agree on the same date.
The documents a broker must keep for each transaction, per the Commission's checklist, for four years.

The written statement of the broker's relationship with a party, required before confidential information is discussed. It is made in a signed engagement contract or on a Commission brokerage disclosure form (to buyer, tenant, seller or landlord).
